# OpenBot Copy

## When To Use

Any string a person reads: a heading, a description, a button, a placeholder, an empty state, a
notice, a chat card, a server error that the browser shows. Server messages count: a 409 that says
what to do next is read by a person as much as any screen is.

Not text written for the model. Tool descriptions, standing instructions and prompts steer how a Bot
behaves, and changing their wording is a behaviour change with its own review. Not code comments,
and not `docs/`, which has its own register.

## The Glossary

One word for one thing, everywhere a person can see it.

| Say | For | Not |
|---|---|---|
| **Bot**, **Bots** (capitalised) | What a person creates, talks to and gives work to. | agent, coworker, assistant, AI |
| **agent** | Only an outside framework's program, in the places that are about connecting one: "an agent you already run", "AG-UI agent". | Bot, when the thing is a Bot |
| **app** | A service a Bot uses: Gmail, Google Drive, Notion. | connector, integration, plugin |
| **Connections** | The page that lists the apps and accounts every Bot uses as you: the every-Bot page of Apps. On a Bot's page the same thing is the **Apps** row. | connected accounts, linked accounts |
| **connect / disconnect / reconnect** | What a person does to their own account. | link (except GitHub and Slack identity, where "link" is the vendor's own word) |
| **skill** | A named instruction invoked with `/`. | command, prompt |
| **admin** | The person who runs OpenBot for everybody. | administrator, owner, operator |
| **OpenBot** | The product the person is using, and their account with it: "Sign in to OpenBot", "your OpenBot account". | this deployment, the server, the instance, CopilotKit |
| **OpenBot by CopilotKit** | The company, only where it has to be named: the license agreement's name, a legal or privacy line, the one place setup says who makes OpenBot. | CopilotKit alone |
| **turn on / turn off** | An admin switching an app or a feature. | enable / disable (in sentences; a switch may still read "Enabled") |
| **conversation** | A thread with one or more Bots. | channel, chat (in sentences) |
| **front end** | The part of OpenBot a person opens in the browser. | the web app, the UI |
| **backend** | The part of OpenBot that runs the Bots and keeps conversations, memory, learning and Skills. One word, "Backend" at the start of a sentence. | back end, Intelligence, CopilotKit Intelligence, the platform, the stack, cpki |
| **backend dashboard** | The backend's own pages, where Learning and projects are managed. | the Intelligence dashboard |
| **database** | Where OpenBot keeps its data. | Postgres (outside Admin) |
| **the computers Bots work on**, **Bot computer** | Where a Bot browses and works with files. | sandbox, container |

### The eight, Setup and Vault

A person learns one noun, Bot, and eight things a Bot has (`docs/how-openbot-works.md`). Wherever
they are listed they keep this order, and a list leaves out one with nothing to set there rather
than showing an empty row. `app/src/lib/primitives.ts` holds the names, the order and the icons.

| Say | For | Not |
|---|---|---|
| **Conversations** | Where you give a Bot work and it reports back. Not a settings row. | channels, groups, chats |
| **Routines** | Work a Bot starts by itself: what, starts, does, until. One list per Bot. A goal is a routine with an outcome to reach; a check-in is a routine that only tells you. | Goals, Check-ins, Responsibilities (as page or menu names) |
| **Memory** | What a Bot knows about you and your work. | Capabilities |
| **Skills** | What a Bot knows how to do: skills you wrote, taught, or OpenBot proposed. One page per scope. | Learning (as a page), What it can do, Skills and access, Capabilities |
| **Apps** | The services a Bot can reach. Connections is its every-Bot page. | Plugins, What it can do |
| **Computer** | Where a Bot browses, runs commands and keeps files, and the folders on your machine it may use. | Browsers, This computer (as pages) |
| **Approvals** | When a Bot stops and asks you. | Approval rules (as a page) |
| **Activity** | The record of what a Bot did. | Audit |
| **Setup** | A Bot's name and instructions. | |
| **Vault** | Your saved logins and keys. No Bot sees what is in it. | Saved logins, Passwords, Keys, Credentials (as pages) |

The scopes are **this Bot** (the Bot's page), **every Bot** (Settings, and Connections for Apps)
and, in the team edition, **everyone** (Admin). The words in the "Not" column may still appear in a
sentence ("a goal", "a check-in", "your saved logins") and as a label inside a page. They are not
the title of a page, a menu entry, or a row that opens one.
`tests/no-retired-page-names.test.ts` reads every such title.

**Never say Intelligence.** To a person, admins included, it is all OpenBot. Name the part of
OpenBot instead: "The backend is starting.", "Waiting for the backend", "Couldn't reach the
backend. Try again." Name a feature by what it does (Automatic learning, Memory, Skills), and say
"OpenBot proposes skills", not who inside OpenBot does. An env var an admin sets keeps its name
(`INTELLIGENCE_API_URL`); the word on its own does not appear. Logs, comments, code and the operator
docs under `docs/` and `charts/` are not shown to a person and may name it.
`tests/no-intelligence-in-user-copy.test.ts` fails on a shown string that says it.

**OpenBot Desktop's first screen says self-contained.** "This version of OpenBot is fully
self-contained and runs entirely on your computer, including the OpenBot backend." The Account
step after it says only what it is for: "OpenBot needs a free license key. Sign in to get one."
Neither names Intelligence.

**Never "CopilotKit" alone.** Product copy says OpenBot, or "OpenBot by CopilotKit" where the
company has to be named. Addresses (`dashboard.copilotkit.ai`, `github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot`),
code identifiers, env names, log lines and Copy diagnostics keep their spelling.
tests/no-intelligence-in-user-copy.test.ts and tests/plain-setup-words.test.ts hold every screen to it.

**Admin is allowed exact names.** An admin page may name `COMPOSIO_API_KEY`, OAuth and "deployment",
because the admin is the one who sets them. A page anybody can open may not.

## The Style

1. **Say what happened, then what to do.** "Gmail isn't connected. Connect it to let Bots read your
   mail." Not why the screen is built the way it is.
2. **Use complete sentences for explanations.** Page descriptions, helper text, notices, and empty-state bodies need a subject and a verb, or a direct instruction ("Connect your accounts"). Avoid fragments such as "The apps your Bots use" or "What this Bot can do." Headings, labels, buttons, and short status labels may be fragments.
   **Keep only useful explanation.** State the action, outcome, or constraint the person needs. Remove copy that merely repeats the heading. Use natural sentence lengths; do not chop prose into fragments to meet a word count.
3. **Plain words.** "use", not "hold a grant on". "can't", not "is unable to". Contractions are fine.

# OpenBot Data Access

## When To Use

This skill applies to any change under `app/src` that moves data between the browser and the API
server. It fires on new screens, new endpoints, new query keys, on any change to `api/openapi.yaml`,
and on any diff that introduces `fetch` anywhere but `app/src/lib/client.ts`.

It does not cover server handlers under `server/`, zod form schemas (`lib/<entity>/form.ts`), or page
layout. It does cover `lib/copilot/`: the conversation itself streams over AG-UI, but the tool calls a
Bot makes during a turn are ordinary authenticated requests and go through the client like everything
else.

## API First

OpenBot's API is described in `api/openapi.yaml` (OpenAPI 3.1), and that file is the single source of
truth: the browser's client, its types, the server's types, the docs and the contract tests all come
from it. It follows CopilotKit Intelligence's v2 conventions so the two read as one API: every
resource under `/api/v2/organizations/{organizationId}/`, errors as `application/problem+json`, lists
paged with `cursor` and `limit` (answering `nextCursor`), and an `Idempotency-Key` on every write.

Resources move into the spec one at a time. Bots are in it (list, create, read, change, delete);
everything else is still reached the older way, through `client`, until its turn. So there are two
kinds of request, and which one a call is depends only on whether its operation is in the spec:

1. **An operation in the spec** is called through the function Orval generated for it
   (`listBots`, `createBot`, …, in `@/lib/api/generated/<tag>/<tag>`), with types from
   `@/lib/api/generated/model`. Never `client(path, …)`, never a hand-written type for its payload.
2. **Anything else** goes through `client` exactly as described below.

The generated functions all run through `apiRequest` in `lib/api/request.ts` (Orval's mutator), which
is built on `clientRequest` in `lib/client.ts`: the same session cookie, and a refusal is the same
`ClientError` carrying the server's own sentence (`error` today, `detail` in problem details) or the
`fallback` the caller passes. A screen cannot tell which kind of request it made.

The generated code is checked in. CI regenerates it and fails when it differs, lints the spec, and
fails a pull request that breaks a client of the base branch's spec (oasdiff).

## The Shape

Every entity the browser knows about owns a directory under `app/src/lib/`:

```
api/openapi.yaml           # the contract
app/src/lib/
  client.ts                # the only fetch in the app
  api/
    request.ts             # Orval's mutator: apiRequest, ORGANIZATION_ID, idempotencyKey()
    served-today.ts        # where today's server answers a spec operation, until it serves /api/v2
    generated/             # Orval's output: functions, hooks, types, Zod schemas, MSW handlers
  <entity>/
    queries.ts   # read types, key factory, queryOptions factories
    mutations.ts # input type, mutationOptions factories
    form.ts      # zod schema (a different skill's territory)
```

`client.ts` owns the transport: credentials, the JSON content type, body serialisation, and turning a
failed status into an `Error` carrying the server's own message. It owns nothing about meaning — the
envelope key and the sentence a person reads stay at the call site, because those are facts about one
endpoint rather than about requests in general.

```ts
client<T>(path, key, options?): Promise<T>    // parsed, and `key` unwrapped
client(path, options?): Promise<Response>     // for a caller that only needed it to work
tryClient(path, options?): Promise<Response>  // never throws; the status is the answer
```

`options` is `{ method?, body?, fallback?, signal? }`. `body` is serialised by the client, which is
also what sets the content type — so a caller passes an object, never a string. Passing
`JSON.stringify(x)` sends a JSON string of a JSON string, which no endpoint accepts.

### Three kinds of request

Not everything crossing the wire is cached state, and the shape follows from which kind it is.

1. **A cached read** is a `queryOptions` factory in `queries.ts`. It has a key, and something can
   invalidate it.
2. **A write somebody asked for** is a `mutationOptions` factory in `mutations.ts`. It invalidates on
   success.
3. **Everything else is a plain exported function**, living beside the factories for its entity.
   A verdict about this moment (`decideComponent`, `testAgentConnection`), a tool call during a
   Bot's turn (`callPluginTool`, the computer control surface), a frame of a screen, a step inside
   another write (`storeMcpToken`). These fail closed and return a value rather than throwing,
   because a refusal is usually the answer. Giving one a cache key would create a key nothing reads
   and an invalidation nothing triggers.

The third kind still lives under `lib/`. It is not licence to call the server from a component.

There are thirteen of these today — `agents`, `audit`, `auth`, `channels`, `components`, `computers`,
`connectors`, `credentials`, `package`, `plugins`, `sandboxed`, `skills`, `copilot`. They all look the
same on purpose. `lib/agents/queries.ts` and `lib/agents/mutations.ts` are the reference pair; read them
before writing a new one.

**The one rule that matters:** a React component never calls `fetch`. If a component file contains
`fetch`, the change is wrong regardless of whether it works.

**And its companion:** a component never imports from `lib/api/generated` either. The generated
functions are called from the entity's factories, which give the result the entity's own cache key.
The generated `use*` hooks and `get*QueryOptions` key their cache by URL, which no `<entity>Keys.all`
invalidation reaches, so a screen on a generated hook shows a second, stale copy of data the
factories already hold.

## Procedures

### Procedure 0: Add or change an operation in the spec

1. Write it in `api/openapi.yaml` first, before any client or server code. Copy the shape of an
   operation already there: the shared `OrganizationId`, `Limit`, `Cursor` and `IdempotencyKey`
   parameters, a `Problem` response for every 4xx and 5xx, `security` naming who may call it. Describe
   what the server does; never invent a field it does not return.
2. `bun run api:lint`. It refuses a path outside `/api/v2/organizations/{organizationId}/`, a path
   Intelligence already serves (`api/intelligence-reserved.yaml`), a write with no `Idempotency-Key`,
   an error that is not problem details, and a list that does not page.
3. `bun run api:generate`, and commit the spec and `app/src/lib/api/generated` together. Never edit a
   generated file: change the spec and generate again.
4. Call the new function from the entity's factory (Procedures 1 and 2): pass `ORGANIZATION_ID`, a

# OpenBot Screen Layout

## When To Use

This skill applies to any change under `app/src/routes` that puts a configuration screen on the
screen — a new admin page, a new settings section, a new row on an existing page, a detail page
behind a list. Twelve screens render through `PageShell` today and seven build their rows out of
`Item`; all of them look the same on purpose.

It does not cover where the data comes from — that is `openbot-data-access`, which owns queries,
mutations, and the pending/error/empty/rows branching. It does not cover the gallery components
under `components/gallery`, which a Bot draws inside a conversation rather than a person navigating
to. It does not cover the primitives under `components/ui`, which are this repository's own design-system
primitives: they began as shadcn output, but there is no upstream to re-pull from, and they are
formatted and linted like the rest of the app.

## The Default

**A new screen uses this layout. Deviating from it needs a reason given in the request.**

This is the point of the skill. The decisions here — the width, the spacing, the heading sizes, the
row anatomy, which control means what — are already made, and they are already made the same way on
every other screen. Somebody who does not work in the frontend should be able to add a page that
looks like it belongs without making a single visual decision, by reaching for `PageShell`,
`PageSection`, `PageRows` and `Item` and filling them in.

The failure this prevents is the one the `PageShell` doc comment describes: Admin was once nine pages
that shared no layout — four container widths, four heading sizes, four padding schemes, three of
them drawing their own buttons and inputs. It did not read as a different screen, it read as a
different application, at exactly the moment an administrator was deciding whether to trust it with
credentials.

So: no hand-drawn containers, no new widths, no new spacing scale, no second way to draw a row. If
the screen genuinely does not fit — a table, a canvas, an editor beside a live preview — that is a
deviation worth stating out loud and worth a comment saying why.

## The Shape

Four components make the frame. They compose in this order and nest no other way.

```
PageShell        the page: header (title, description, action, backButton) then children
  PageSection    a titled group of unrelated decisions, with a deliberately large gap above it
    PageRows     the grouped card: rounded-lg border bg-card
      Item       one row, size="sm", divided from its neighbours by <Separator />
    PageEmpty    what a section says when it has nothing to list
```

`PageShell` takes a `width`: `prose` (`max-w-3xl`, 768px) is the default, and every
configuration screen uses it so no screen is wider than another. Sentences inside it are held to
`max-w-prose`, so the column has room for a label beside its control without stretching the text.
`wide` (`max-w-5xl`) exists for one screen — `admin/audit.tsx`, because an audit log is a table to be
scanned and prose width would wrap every row. It is not a licence for anything else to be wide.

## The Rhythm

Spacing comes from the frame, not from the screen. These are the gaps every screen gets by using the
components above; a screen that sets its own is drifting.

| Between | Gap | Where it lives |
|---------|-----|----------------|
| Page edge (top / sides / bottom) | 48 / 16 / 64px | `PageShell` column (`pt-12` or `pt-8` under the bar, `px-4`, `pb-16`) |
| Title → description | 8px | `PageShell` header |
| Title block → first content | 32px | `PageShell`: `[&>header+*]:mt-8` |
| Title → tabs, tabs → content | 24px, then 32px | `PageShell`: `[&>header+nav]`, `[&>header+nav+*]` |
| Section → section | 48px | `PageSection` (`mt-12`) |
| Section heading → description | 4px | `PageSection` |
| Heading block → section content | 16px | `PageRows` / `PageEmpty` (`mt-4`) |
| Controls stacked inside a section | 12px | the screen, with `gap-3` |
| A row in `PageRows` | 65px with a description, never under 56px | `Item` (`px-4 py-3.5 gap-3`), `PageRows` (`min-h-14`) |
| Divider between rows | inset 16px from both edges | `PageRows`, on every horizontal `Separator` inside it |

The 32px under the title is deliberately tighter than the 48px between sections: the title belongs
to the page it introduces. Those `PageShell` selectors outrank the first child's own `mt-*`, so a
section or notice keeps its usual margin everywhere else and loses it only at the top.

A page with one section gives that section no `title`: the page title already names it, and a second
heading 32px below the first says the same thing twice. Put the description on `PageShell` instead
(`connections.index.tsx`). A count or filter that belongs to a search sits on the search's row, not
on a line of its own.

`PageEmpty` is shadcn's empty state: a bordered box where the rows would be, with an `icon` for
the kind of thing, a `title` ("No rules yet", "No matches", "Background research is off"), one
sentence of description saying how the first one arrives, and an `action` — the same Add button the
page already has — when there is one to offer. Don't repeat "Add one with X" in the description when
the action is right there. A search with no results uses `IconSearch` and "No matches".

## Procedures

### Procedure 1: Lay out a screen

1. Open with `PageShell`, giving it `title` and `description`. Leave `width` alone.
2. On a detail screen reached from a list, pass `backButton={{ label, linkProps }}` — it draws a
   chevron-left bar above the header. Do not put a Back button in `action`; `action` is for the
   page's one primary verb, on the title's baseline.
3. Group the page's decisions into `PageSection`s, each with a `title` and, where the grouping is not
   self-evident, a `description`.
4. Give each section one `PageRows` card. Rows go inside it as `Item size="sm"`, with `<Separator />`
   between them and none after the last. `PageRows` is a card with dividers, not a stack of cards —
   gaps between rows are the wrong shape.
5. Read `admin/plugins/index.tsx` for the whole pattern end to end, and
   `admin/plugins/$key.tsx` or `admin/components/$name.tsx` for a screen with several sections and
   mixed row kinds.

### Procedure 2: Compose a row

1. `ItemMedia variant="icon"` holds a leading icon from `@tabler/icons-react`, drawn as a 16px glyph
   on a 32px muted tile. It is what makes a card of rows scannable; a row without one reads as a
   paragraph. Pass the bare icon — the variant sizes and colours it — and use plain `ItemMedia` only
   for something that is its own picture, such as a Bot's avatar.
2. `ItemContent` holds `ItemTitle` and, where the row needs a second line, `ItemDescription`.
3. `ItemActions` holds the control, or the value when the row is read-only.
4. `ItemHeader` and `ItemFooter` are `basis-full`, so they wrap onto a line of their own inside the
   row. That is where a **set** goes — chips, toggles, anything that would otherwise fight the label
   for horizontal space. A set does not belong in `ItemActio
